query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A trace addition of Nb introduced during alloy synthesis promotes its preferential segregation to lamellar colony boundaries, reinforcing these interfaces to delay microcrack initiation and propagation, which will simultaneously improve both yield strength and room-temperature tensile ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys that exhibit a dual-phase lamellar microstructure with numerous internal boundaries, where weak interlamellar interfaces trigger microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, small concentration of Nb during alloy production so that, with appropriate cooling and heat treatments, Nb segregates selectively to the lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.conditions: Processing conditions must include controlled solidification and post-solidification heat treatments that facilitate Nb segregation to boundaries; the alloy is subsequently subjected to uniaxial tensile deformation at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, Nb-enriched interfacial layer forms along the lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Nb segregation increases the cohesive strength of the formerly weak colony interfaces, reducing the local stress concentrations that lead to microcrack formation. At the same time, it does not impede dislocation motion within the lamellae, thereby reconciling the trade-off between strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventional eutectic HEAs with unmodified boundaries, the Nb-modified alloy is expected to exhibit higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths together with enhanced elongation at failure during room-temperature tensile tests.
generation.baseline: Conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar microstructures where unmodified, weak interlamellar boundaries lead to early microcracking and limited ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only if the Nb addition is maintained at trace levels and processing parameters are optimized to ensure selective interfacial segregation without triggering deleterious secondary phase formation; exceeding these thresholds may lead to embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvements in strength and ductility depends on precise Nb concentration and processing conditions, and remains to be quantitatively established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples using identical processing conditions: one control set without Nb addition and one test set with a trace amount of Nb added. Apply the same heat treatment to promote Nb segregation. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to confirm the formation of Nb-enriched interfacial layers, and perform room-temperature tensile tests to compare yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility between the two sets.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-doped alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the control, or if microstructural analysis does not verify the formation of a continuous Nb-enriched interfacial layer, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a modest amount of a microalloying element (for example, Nb) to promote interlamellar interface modification will simultaneously enhance strength and room‐temperature tensile ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys by strengthening and toughening the weak colony boundaries.
drafts.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous, comparatively weak internal boundaries where microcracks initiate during room-temperature tensile deformation.
drafts.intervention: Add a controlled, small concentration of Nb (or a functionally similar element) during alloy synthesis to encourage its segregation to the lamellar colony boundaries.
drafts.conditions: Processing must be tuned so that the microalloying element selectively segregates to colony boundaries without forming deleterious bulk brittle phases; the test should be conducted under room-temperature tensile conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: A thin, ductile Nb-enriched interfacial film at the lamellar boundaries, which may also generate nanoscale Nb-rich precipitates within the matrix.
drafts.mechanism: During solidification and subsequent thermomechanical processing, the microalloying element is driven to the colony boundaries where it forms a cohesive interfacial layer. This film reinforces the weak links between lamellae, increasing the cohesive energy at these critical interfaces, thus delaying microcrack initiation and propagation. In addition, any fine Nb-rich precipitates contribute to precipitation strengthening, thereby enhancing the overall strength.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified baseline, the intervention is predicted to yield an alloy with increased yield and ultimate tensile strengths and improved ductility (higher elongation to fracture) under room-temperature tensile loading.
drafts.baseline: Conventional eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colony structure that exhibits inherent brittleness under tensile deformation due to weak interlamellar interfaces.
drafts.boundary: The positive effect is expected only if the Nb concentration and processing conditions are optimized to ensure selective interfacial segregation without triggering the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds; exceeding or mismanaging these parameters could lead to grain boundary embrittlement.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples using identical processing routes: one set with the optimized Nb microalloying treatment and one control set without Nb addition. Ensure that processing conditions promote interfacial segregation in the treated samples. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests accompanied by detailed microstructural examinations (e.g., using TEM or SEM) to verify the presence and integrity of the Nb-enriched interfacial layer.
measurements: Mechanical properties: yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to fracture
Microstructural characterization of lamellar boundaries (TEM/SEM) to detect Nb-rich films and precipitates
Phase identification to rule out the formation of unwanted brittle phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-microalloyed samples do not display a statistically significant improvement in both strength (yield/ultimate tensile strength) and tensile ductility (elongation to fracture) compared to the control, or if microstructural analysis fails to verify the formation of a continuous Nb-enriched interfacial layer or shows the emergence of detrimental brittle phases, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Adding a trace alloying element (such as Nb) that segregates preferentially to lamellar colony boundaries will modify the interfacial structure to suppress microcrack initiation and propagation, thereby simultaneously improving both strength and room‐temperature ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
drafts.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar colonies having numerous internal boundaries that act as crack initiation sites under tensile loading.
drafts.intervention: Introduce a small, controlled concentration of Nb during alloy production so that upon solidification and subsequent heat treatment, Nb segregates to the internal (colony) boundaries.
drafts.conditions: Use processing conditions (e.g., controlled cooling and post-solidification annealing) that promote Nb segregation to the lamellar interfaces; testing at room temperature under uniaxial tensile deformation.
drafts.structural_mediator: Modified interfacial chemistry/structure at the lamellar colony boundaries in which Nb forms a thin, stable interfacial phase that alters local bonding and reduces stress concentrations.
drafts.mechanism: The Nb segregation at colony boundaries is expected to enhance boundary cohesion and reduce the propensity for microcrack nucleation. By impeding crack propagation while still allowing for dislocation motion within the lamellae, the intervention promotes both higher strength (by restricting premature failure at weak boundaries) and greater ductility (by allowing more uniform plastic accommodation).
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified, conventionally processed alloy, the Nb-modified alloy is predicted to exhibit higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths along with increased elongation at failure during room-temperature tensile tests.
drafts.baseline: Conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloys with unmodified lamellar colonies, which typically display high strength accompanied by limited ductility due to microcrack formation at internal boundaries.
drafts.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only under processing conditions that result in effective Nb segregation without forming unwanted secondary phases. The hypothesis may not hold if the Nb concentration is too high (leading to brittle intermetallic formation) or if processing temperatures/times do not allow for adequate segregation kinetics.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples: a control set using conventional processing and a test set with a trace addition of Nb. Apply identical heat treatments designed to encourage Nb segregation. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and atom probe tomography (APT) to confirm Nb segregation at the colony boundaries. Perform room-temperature tensile tests to compare yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility (elongation to failure) between the two sets.
measurements: Microstructural characterization of colony boundaries (via TEM/APT)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-doped alloy does not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility (e.g., less than a 5% improvement relative to the baseline) or if Nb is not confirmed to segregate preferentially at the lamellar boundaries, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A hybrid thermo‐mechanical processing step that induces serrated phase boundaries and in‐situ twin formation within the dual-phase lamellar colonies of eutectic HEAs will simultaneously impede microcrack nucleation and enhance dislocation/twin interactions, thereby improving both room‐temperature tensile strength and ductility relative to the as‐cast microstructure.
drafts.material_initial_state: An as‐cast eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring dual-phase (e.g., soft FCC and hard B2 or ordered intermetallic) lamellar colonies with relatively smooth internal boundaries that serve as initiation sites for microcracks during room-temperature tensile deformation.
drafts.intervention: Apply a controlled hybrid thermo-mechanical treatment—specifically, an initial cryogenic cold rolling to store deformation energy (and promote twin formation) followed by a moderate-temperature warm rolling (or partial annealing) to induce serration of the colony/phase boundaries.
drafts.conditions: Room-temperature tensile testing conditions after processing; processing parameters must be tuned to avoid excessive grain refinement or phase decomposition.
drafts.structural_mediator: The formation of serrated phase boundaries along with retained deformation twins within the lamellar colonies.
drafts.mechanism: Serrated boundaries increase the resistance to crack initiation and propagation by distributing local stress concentrations more evenly, while the induced twins act as both obstacles to dislocation motion (enhancing strength) and sites for additional strain hardening (improving ductility).
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified as-cast lamellar HEA, the treated alloy will exhibit an increase in yield and ultimate tensile strengths along with a higher elongation to failure due to delayed microcrack coalescence and enhanced plastic deformation mechanisms.
drafts.baseline: The original as-cast eutectic HEA with smooth dual-phase lamellar colonies, known to develop microcracks at internal boundaries that limit room-temperature ductility.
drafts.boundary: This improvement is expected when the processing window is restricted to conditions that promote boundary serration and twin retention without causing unwanted phase transformations or excessive grain refinement. The hypothesis applies to eutectic HEAs with dual-phase lamellar microstructures as described.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens of the eutectic HEA: one set processed with the conventional casting and minimal post-treatment (baseline) and a second set subjected to the hybrid thermo-mechanical treatment (cryo-rolling followed by controlled warm rolling/partial annealing). Conduct standardized room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests on both sets. Use microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/EBSD and TEM) to verify the presence of serrated boundaries and retained twins in the treated samples compared to the smoother boundaries in the baseline.
measurements: Fracture analysis (to detect microcrack initiation sites)
Microstructural imaging to quantify boundary serration and twin density
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not show statistically significant improvements in both strength and ductility—e.g., less than a 20% increase in yield/ultimate strength or ductility relative to the baseline—or if microstructural analysis does not confirm the expected changes (serrated boundaries and increased twin density), then the hypothesis will be falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount of Hf into the eutectic high‐entropy alloy will promote the formation of finely distributed Hf‐rich precipitates at the lamellar colony boundaries, which will simultaneously reinforce the interface to impede microcrack initiation while also enhancing strength by precipitation and pinning effects; this dual role will result in both improved room‐temperature tensile strength and ductility compared to the unmodified alloy.
drafts.material_initial_state: A eutectic high‐entropy alloy with a dual-phase lamellar microstructure (e.g., an AlCoCrFeNi2.1-type alloy) where soft and hard phases coexist and microcracks tend to initiate along numerous internal lamellar colony boundaries during room-temperature tensile deformation.
drafts.intervention: Alloying with a trace amount (e.g., ~0.5 at%) of Hf added during alloy preparation.
drafts.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation conditions, with conventional casting and subsequent thermo-mechanical processing used to retain the eutectic lamellar morphology.
drafts.structural_mediator: Hf-rich precipitates that form at and along the lamellar colony boundaries.
drafts.mechanism: The trace Hf addition is expected to nucleate finely dispersed Hf-rich phases at the internal boundaries. These precipitates increase the cohesive strength at the interfaces (interface pinning), reducing the susceptibility for microcrack initiation while providing precipitation strengthening. This dual effect is anticipated to raise the overall tensile strength and simultaneously improve ductility by delaying catastrophic crack propagation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline unmodified eutectic alloy, the Hf-doped alloy should exhibit higher yield and ultimate tensile strengths along with increased elongation (ductility) during room-temperature tensile tests.
drafts.baseline: An unmodified eutectic high-entropy alloy with its typical dual-phase lamellar microstructure, which suffers from early microcrack initiation at the numerous internal boundaries leading to brittleness.
drafts.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected if the Hf addition is kept at a trace level (around 0.5 at%) so that the overall lamellar morphology is preserved and no large-scale phase transformation occurs; the intervention is limited to alloys whose processing conditions enable the controlled precipitation of Hf-rich phases at the boundaries.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples with identical processing conditions: one set of the baseline eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) and another set with an added ~0.5 at% Hf. Characterize the microstructure using SEM/TEM to verify the presence and distribution of Hf-rich precipitates at the internal boundaries. Then conduct room-temperature tensile tests on both sets to measure yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation.
measurements: Microstructure analysis (SEM/TEM) to assess the formation and location of Hf-rich precipitates
Room-temperature tensile tests to obtain yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and percent elongation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf-doped samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility relative to the baseline samples—or if the addition of Hf disrupts the dual-phase lamellar morphology such that microcrack initiation is not reduced—then the hypothesis is falsified.
